Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

REFERENCE NOTES — depot delivery episode

At North Quay Depot, receiving clerk Mara Venn coordinates the morning handoff with the small dispatch team. The depot sits beside the old ferry road, and its covered loading bay has three marked lanes. Deliveries arrive throughout the day, but the first shift usually handles the paperwork before the afternoon crew takes over. Mara keeps a paper notebook for unusual arrivals because the shared screen is not always available near the outer doors. Her supervisor, Dev Patel, checks the daily handoff notes before leaving at four.

On Tuesday, a van from Alder Supply reached the depot shortly after the gate opened. The driver waited while two pallets were moved out of lane one, then handed Mara a manifest and a revised packing slip. Mara wrote down the arrival time and noted that the slip showed a different carton count from the manifest. She said, “I can record what’s here now, but I need the paperwork discrepancy to stay visible for the next shift.” The driver signed the gate sheet and left a copy of the revised slip with the receiving desk.

A second delivery came from Bracken Foods just before lunch. One crate had a damp corner, but the seal was intact and the label could still be read. The team placed the crate on a separate trolley while Dev took a photograph for the supplier file. He told Mara, “Keep the condition note with the delivery record; the photo alone won’t tell the afternoon crew where the crate went.” The crate remained in the marked inspection area until the warehouse lead could check it.

Later that afternoon, a scheduled vehicle from Cinder Paper arrived after its appointment window. It carried several bundles for two different storage aisles, and the driver asked whether both could be unloaded at once. Mara checked the lane board and directed the crew to clear one aisle first so the second bundle would not block the route to the emergency exit. The delay was written in the shift notebook. The delivery was handled at the depot, but the notes do not say when each bundle was put away.

The depot’s handoff practice changed after a busy Friday earlier in the month. At that time, a temporary worker had copied a unit count from a preliminary slip before the final paperwork arrived. Dev later clarified that a preliminary count should remain marked as provisional until the signed delivery documents are available. Mara recalled his wording as, “A number on an early slip is useful, but it isn’t the same thing as a confirmed receipt.” No one changed the older notebook entry; the correction was written beside it, with the date and the worker’s initials.

During the next week, the team used a yellow tag for packages that needed follow-up. The tag recorded the depot lane, the delivery reference, and the name of the person taking the next action. It did not replace the normal receipt paperwork. If a package was moved before its paperwork was complete, the person moving it was asked to update the tag as well as tell the receiving clerk. Mara said that this condition mattered most during shift changes, when the person who first saw a package might no longer be on site.

A short operations meeting took place on Thursday in the break room. Dev, Mara, and warehouse lead Inez Cole compared the handoff notebook with the gate sheet. Inez pointed out that the two records answer different practical questions: the gate sheet helps staff trace vehicle arrival, while the notebook records exceptions that affect the work inside the depot. Dev said, “Let’s not read a missing note as proof that nothing happened.” The team agreed to keep both records in their existing locations and to bring questions about unclear entries to the next shift lead.

1. The morning handoff is managed by Mara, with Dev reviewing notes before his shift ends. The afternoon crew relies on the handoff record when an arrival, paperwork issue, or package location needs follow-up.
2. The Alder Supply paperwork showed a mismatch between the manifest and revised slip. The Bracken Foods crate had a damp corner with an intact seal and was placed in an inspection area. These are separate events, and the notes do not say that either issue was resolved.
3. The Cinder Paper vehicle arrived after its appointment window. The crew unloaded in an order chosen to keep the emergency-exit route clear; the notes do not provide a final put-away time for either bundle.
4. A preliminary unit count is to remain provisional until signed delivery documents are available. The yellow follow-up tag is used alongside ordinary receipt paperwork, not instead of it. If an incompletely documented package is moved, the tag should be updated and the receiving clerk told.
5. The gate sheet and handoff notebook serve different purposes. The team kept both records in their existing locations, and unclear entries were to be raised with the next shift lead.
